parent.name: Philidor Defense: Exchange Variation
parent.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 exd4 4. Nxd4
parent.overview: After 3.d4 exd4 White recaptures (4.Nxd4 is the main line; Morphy's 4.Qxd4 is the alternative) and then has a space advantage and the more comfortable game. Black replies ...Nf6 and ...Be7, castles quickly and aims for a compact position (often with ...Nbd7 or ...c5/...c6 later) with king safety first, using ...d5 or ...c5 as freeing breaks. The structure is passive but not refuted: White cannot force a tactical win, but must prove an edge. Sources call it a sound, practical defence, an easy entry point for club players that is rarely used by top players because it concedes space; Aronian is mentioned as an occasional user. The Antoshin set-up (6.Be2) is a common White try.

parent.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Modern Defense
parent.overview: Against 1.d4 Black plays 1...g6, fianchettoing the king's bishop (...Bg7) and delaying the knight on f6 and any central commitment. The idea is hypermodern: let White build a pawn centre, then attack it from the flanks with ...d6 and ...c5 or ...e5, with queenside play (...b5, ...a5) backed by the Bg7. Because ...Nf6 is delayed it can still become a King's Indian (after c4 and Nc3), a Pirc (after e4) or a Grünfeld, or stay a separate Modern. White's common set-ups are a classical centre (c4, e4, Nc3, Be3), the Averbakh with c4, or the pseudo-Austrian or Samisch-like f4/f3 centres with a kingside space attack. Sources disagree on the character: the line is balanced and sound but can become very sharp and awkward for Black if the kingside weakens.

parent.name: King's Indian Defense: Normal Variation
parent.moves: 1. d4 Nf6 2. c4 g6 3. Nc3 Bg7 4. e4 d6 5. Be2
parent.overview: This root is the King's Indian reached by the move order 1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.c4 (the same position as 3.Nf3 in the 2.c4 move order). It is not a distinct opening: it is the ordinary King's Indian, where Black fianchettoes with ...Bg7, castles, and strikes at White's centre with ...e5, ...c5 or ...f5. White's choice of set-up decides the character: the classical 4.Nc3 and e4 leads to the locked-centre opposite-wing race (c4-c5 against ...f5-f4), while the Fianchetto Variation (g3, Bg2, O-O, Nc3) is quieter, positional, and has less forcing theory. The data subtree groups 4.e4 Normal Variation lines (the majority of games) under this root, so it mixes both. Black's success depends on timing and coordination rather than automatic aggression.

parent.name: Sicilian Defense: Open
parent.moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4
parent.overview: After 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Black has developed the knight to c6 before choosing a set-up, so the root is a crossroads: Classical (5.Nc3 d6), Sveshnikov (5...e5 after ...Nf6), Four Knights (5...e6), Kalashnikov or Lowenthal (4...e5), Accelerated Dragon (4...g6) and Taimanov-type lines (s1, s2, s3). White gets a development lead and kingside space, Black gets the open c-file and a central pawn majority, so the play is unbalanced and complex (s1). The Richter-Rauzer (6.Bg5) and Sozin (6.Bc4) lead to a race where White attacks on the kingside, often castling queenside, and Black counters with ...a6, ...b5 and c-file pressure (s2). Statistics are balanced (White 47.7%, Black 47.3% in 5.6 million Lichess games, per the Chessiverse page for the Four Knights) (s3).

parent.name: English Opening
parent.overview: White opens with the c-pawn to contest d5 from the wing, keeping the e4, d4, g3 and b3 options open until Black reveals a set-up. It is a flexible, hypermodern, mostly positional opening: not as sharp as 1.e4 or 1.d4, with the character decided by Black's reply and by transpositions into the Queen's Gambit, Réti or King's Indian. Principal branches are the Reversed Sicilian (1...e5, with an extra tempo for White), the Symmetrical (1...c5, often with a Maroczy bind) and the Anglo-Indian (1...Nf6 and 1...e6/...g6 transpositions). White typically plays Nc3, g3 and Bg2, and expands on the queenside with Rb1 and b4, or takes the classical centre with e4. The database root is a crossroads; its most-played continuations are transpositions to QGD (1.c4 e6 2.Nc3 d5 3.d4), the King's Indian and the Réti.

parent.name: King's Indian Defense: Orthodox Variation
parent.moves: 1. d4 Nf6 2. c4 g6 3. Nc3 Bg7 4. e4 d6 5. Nf3 O-O 6. Be2
parent.overview: Black has allowed White a broad pawn centre (c4, d4, e4) and now contests it with ...e5, the move that defines the Orthodox (Classical) set-up. The main line is 7.O-O Nc6 8.d5 Ne7, the Mar del Plata, where the centre locks and the game becomes a race on opposite wings: Black reroutes the f6-knight, plays ...f5-f4 and ...g5 against the king, while White plays b4/c5 (or the Bayonet 9.b4) to open the queenside before Black's attack lands. 7.d5 (Petrosian) is a slower, positional alternative in which Black plays ...a5 and ...Na6 first; 7...exd4 and 7...Nbd7 lines are older and calmer; ...c5 at move 6 gives a Benoni-like game. The set-up is learned as a pattern (Black plays nearly the same moves each game) but the timing of the pawn storm and the defence against c5 are hard to get right.

parent.name: Ruy Lopez
parent.overview: The Ruy Lopez is the most extensively developed Open Game. 3.Bb5 attacks the knight that defends e5, building indirect pressure on the e5 pawn without the Italian's vulnerability to ...d5. This root (3.Bb5) is a crossroads: after the most common 3...a6 (about two-thirds of games) the Closed Spanish (4.Ba4 Nf6 5.O-O Be7 6.Re1 b5 7.Bb3 d6 8.c3 O-O 9.h3) leads to a slow, locked-centre manoeuvring game; the Berlin (3...Nf6 4.O-O Nxe4) gives a solid, drawish endgame-flavoured structure; the Marshall Attack is a sharp Black pawn sacrifice. White's central plan is c3 and d4 plus the Nbd2-f1-g3 knight route, while Black counterattacks on the queenside (...b5, ...Na5, ...c5) or breaks with ...d5. Theory is the deepest of any 1.e4 opening.
